title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting, from pages 155-157. S is a scheme over a base T and P^∞_{S/T}(M) denotes the sheaf of principal parts (infinite jets) of M. There is a sequence (37), ... → P^∞(E') →u P^∞(E) →v P^∞(E'') → 0, where E carries a stratification relative to T. The stratification gives an O-linear map δ: E → P^∞(E). The Taylor map d^∞: E → P^∞(E) is the infinite-order differential operator. A section e is horizontal exactly when d^∞e = δe.

Torsor data. P' is a torsor under E' and P = P' ×^{E'} E is the pushed-out E-torsor. Previous page: a stratification on P compatible with that of E amounts to a map λ': P' → (P^∞(E)/δE)^♮ with λ'(x'+ξ') = λ'(x') + d^∞(uξ').

The canonical section φ. Compose λ'(x') with v, where x' is any local section of P'. Changing x' to x'+ξ' changes the result by v d^∞ u ξ' = d^∞(v u ξ') = 0. So the local values glue to a global section φ(P,σ) ∈ Γ(S, P^∞(E'')/vδ(E)).

This page first comments on φ. It is not itself an integrable jet of E''. It is the class of such a jet up to the ambiguity vδ(E), i.e. 'defined modulo the image of a section of E''. Classically, φ is the infinite jet of a multivalued 'abelian integral', well defined up to periods.

Picard-Fuchs operators, (39)-(41). Take F a quasi-coherent O_S-module and D: E'' → F a differential operator relative to T. Equivalently, D is an O-linear map u_D: P^∞(E'') → F. D is called a Picard-Fuchs operator for (37) if u_D vanishes on vδ(E), so that it factors through ū_D: P^∞(E'')/vδ(E) → F. Concretely, for any horizontal section e of E, D(v(e)) = u_D(v d^∞ e) = u_D(v δ e) = 0. So D annihilates the E''-components of all horizontal sections ('periods'). This is the classical definition of a Picard-Fuchs equation, phrased intrinsically.

The Gauss-Manin section, (42). Define μ_D(P,σ) := ū_D(φ(P,σ)) ∈ Γ(S,F). The next page names this 'the Gauss-Manin section of F attached to D and (P,σ)'. Hence a Picard-Fuchs operator applied to an integral that is only defined modulo periods yields a genuine global section of F.

The universal version takes values in P^∞(E'')/u Sol(E'). The next page also gives a variant for integrable connections, (43)-(45): operators Δ on E⊗Ω^1 that vanish on d^0_E(u(E')).

Interpretation. This is the abstract, characteristic-free form, phrased with stratifications (infinite-order jets, hence Hasse-type operators in char p), of Manin's construction. In that construction, the Picard-Fuchs operator applied to the abelian integral of a point, or of a torsor/extension, gives a well-defined function: the Manin map μ from torsors (e.g. rational points of an abelian scheme, via torsors under the vector-group part) to Γ(S,F). Manin's map is a homomorphism. Here linearity of μ_D in (P',σ) follows from additivity of λ' under Baer sum of torsors, but this is not stated on the page.
errors: No genuine mathematical error, but a hidden hypothesis is needed. If v were horizontal for stratifications on E and E'', then vδ_E(E) = δ_{E''}(E''). The Picard-Fuchs condition would then just mean that D kills the horizontal sections of E'', and φ would be trivial to obtain. For the construction to have content, E'' must be a quotient of E that is not stratified (e.g. a Hodge-type quotient such as H^1(O) or Lie of the dual), with only the P^∞'s carrying their canonical stratifications. Alternatively, vδ(E) must be read as the jets of the E''-components of horizontal sections of E. The notes leave this implicit ('compatible aux stratifications').

The remark that φ is 'defined modulo the image of a section of E'' is loose. The ambiguity at the level of E is d^∞u(E'). After pushing to E'' it disappears, and what remains is the quotient by vδ(E). Both statements are fine but are conflated in the marginal additions.
Additivity or functoriality of μ_D in the torsor (the Manin homomorphism property) is not stated or checked on this page.

ideas.what: Canonical section φ(P,σ) of P^∞(E'')/vδ(E) attached to a torsor P' under E' with a stratification on P = P'×^{E'}E. It is the infinite jet of a multivalued 'integral' modulo periods.
ideas.modern_name: Jet of a normal function / abelian integral modulo periods; class of an extension of D-modules (crystals)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Manin (1963); the extension-of-D-modules viewpoint is due to Katz, Deligne, Coleman and Chai.

ideas.what: Intrinsic definition of a Picard-Fuchs operator: a differential operator D: E''→F whose linearization P^∞(E'')→F kills vδ(E), i.e. D annihilates the E''-components of all horizontal sections of E.
ideas.modern_name: Picard-Fuchs operator / annihilator of the periods in the D-module generated by a class
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Picard, Fuchs); intrinsic D-module form by Katz-Oda (1968), Manin and Katz.

ideas.what: Gauss-Manin section μ_D(P,σ) = ū_D(φ(P,σ)) ∈ Γ(S,F): a Picard-Fuchs operator applied to an integral defined modulo periods gives a well-defined section.
ideas.modern_name: Manin map (Manin homomorphism), as in the theorem of the kernel
ideas.usually_credited_to: Yu. Manin (1963); rigorous treatments by Coleman (1990), Chai (1991), Bertrand; differential-algebraic version by Buium.

ideas.what: Formulation via stratifications (infinite-order jets P^∞) rather than connections, so that it works in all characteristics. The next page gives the connection variant separately. The dossier is titled with the Cartier operation.
ideas.modern_name: Manin map in positive characteristic via Hasse-Schmidt derivations / stratifications
ideas.usually_credited_to: Voloch, Buium-Voloch (around 1990s) for char p Manin-type maps.

ideas.what: Universal Picard-Fuchs equation with values in the presheaf P^∞(E'')/u Sol(E') (next page).
ideas.modern_name: Universal Manin map / universal differential character

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets up a general, characteristic-free (stratification-based) formalism of the Manin map. Torsors P' under E' inside a stratified E yield a canonical jet modulo periods. Any intrinsically defined Picard-Fuchs operator then turns it into a 'Gauss-Manin section' μ_D(P,σ) ∈ Γ(S,F). The later literature on Manin's theorem of the kernel (Coleman, Chai, Bertrand) and on char-p analogues via Hasse-Schmidt derivations (Voloch, Buium) does not, as far as I know, credit or use such a formalism by Grothendieck.
missed.quote: On dit que D est un opérateur de Picard-Fuchs, relativement à la suite exacte (37), si l'application linéaire correspondante (40) s'annule sur vδ(E) ... μ_D(P,σ) = ū_D(φ(P,σ)) ∈ Γ(S,F)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It gives a uniform definition of the Manin map for arbitrary extensions of stratified modules (crystals) in any characteristic. This is relevant to Mordell-Lang over function fields and to Buium-style differential characters. The version with infinite-order jets is exactly what char p requires.

missed.claim: Homomorphy and functoriality of μ_D in the torsor (Baer sum), and the kernel of μ_D (a 'theorem of the kernel'), are not addressed. These are the key properties of Manin's map, and Coleman later found a gap in Manin's own treatment of them.
missed.quote: on l'appelera la section de Gauss-Manin de F associée à l'op. de Picard-Fuchs D et aux données (P, σ)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A general kernel theorem in this stratified setting would bear on Manin-kernel results in char p.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a clean, unpublished, characteristic-free (stratification-based) abstraction of Manin's Picard-Fuchs/Manin-map construction, with a universal version. The underlying idea is Manin's and is well known, so this is a notable unpublished detail rather than a new theorem.
transcription_corrections: 'P = P'×_{E'} E' should be the contracted product P = P'×^{E'} E, as on the previous page.

'Ce n'est pas H : jet un jet intégrable de E''' is likely 'Ce n'est pas un jet intégrable de E''', mais ... (à des v δ(E) près) ... un tel jet'. The marginal insertion reads roughly 'limite des vδ(E)' / 'l'image d'une section de E''.
'un op. différentiel dans rel./T': the insertion over 'diff.' is probably 'diff.' / 'dans', i.e. 'un op. différentiel rel./T'.
In (38)/(41) the quotient is by vδ(E); the previous page's '/δ(E)' should be read as vδ(E) in P^∞(E'').
